title: An Insult That Started a War
overview: A kind gesture from David is taken as a spy mission, and the insult that follows draws Ammon and its hired allies into a war they lose.

parts.label: Kindness taken as spying (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: David sends envoys to comfort the new Ammonite king, Hanun, because his father Nahash had once been kind to David, though the text does not say how. Hanun's advisers call the envoys spies, and shaving them and cutting their robes to expose them was a deep public humiliation, so David lets them stay out of sight in Jericho until their beards grow back.

parts.label: Ammon hires an army (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: Knowing they have made David their enemy, the Ammonites pay an enormous sum of silver to hire chariots and soldiers from several Aramean kingdoms to the north. Joab, David's army commander, marches out and finds the Ammonites at their city gate while the hired troops wait in the open country.

parts.label: Joab's battle plan (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: Caught between two forces, Joab takes the best troops against the Arameans and gives the rest to his brother Abishai, each promising to rescue the other. He urges courage for their people and towns but leaves the outcome to the LORD, and when the Arameans run, the Ammonites retreat into their city.

parts.label: Arameans regroup and fall (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: The Arameans call in more troops from beyond the Euphrates, but David leads all Israel against them and kills their commander Shophak, after which the defeated kingdoms make peace with David and stop helping Ammon. The casualty numbers differ from the parallel account in 2 Samuel 10, and scholars are unsure whether this comes from copying errors or whether the two accounts are counting different things.

think: When has a gesture of goodwill been read as a threat, and what made the suspicion feel believable at the time?
